clinicalPearls: A syndrome of excessive erythrocytosis and severe hypoxaemia in long-term residents of high altitude
Symptoms include headache, dizziness, breathlessness, sleep disturbance, cyanosis and mental slowing
Marked polycythaemia raises blood viscosity and predisposes to thrombosis and pulmonary hypertension
Over time it can progress to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure (cor pulmonale)
It is distinguished from acute altitude illness by its chronic course in acclimatised long-term dwellers
Descent to lower altitude is the most effective treatment, with phlebotomy and respiratory stimulants as adjuncts
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic mountain sickness develops in some long-term high-altitude residents who lose adequate ventilatory and other adaptations, leading to accentuated hypoxaemia. The chronic hypoxia drives excessive erythropoietin-mediated red-cell production, producing severe polycythaemia that increases blood viscosity and impairs oxygen delivery. Sustained hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular remodelling cause pulmonary hypertension, which ultimately strains the right heart. The combination of hypoxaemia, hyperviscosity and pulmonary hypertension underlies the symptoms and complications.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary polycythaemia from chronic lung or cardiac disease
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count documenting excessive erythrocytosis
Oxygen saturation and arterial blood gas showing hypoxaemia
Echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension and right heart function
Assessment for coexisting sleep-disordered breathing or lung disease
Exclusion of primary polycythaemia where appropriate
redFlags: Signs of right heart failure or severe pulmonary hypertension
Very high haematocrit with hyperviscosity symptoms
reference.prognosis: Symptoms and erythrocytosis typically improve substantially with descent; if residence at altitude continues, progression to pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure worsens the outlook.
pitfalls: Attributing the polycythaemia to a primary haematological disorder
Overlooking coexisting sleep apnoea worsening hypoxaemia
Relying on phlebotomy without addressing altitude exposure
